Queue::series, Queue::note, Queue::timeline, Queue::duration¶

Back to Queue API Reference

Signature¶

const Series& series() const;
Series& series();
const Note& note() const;
Note& note();
const Timeline& timeline() const;
Timeline& timeline();
const Duration& duration() const;
Duration& duration();

What It Does¶

Each accessor returns a reference to the payload, typed as its real type, if the Queue actually holds that kind. Calling the wrong one – note() on a Queue holding a Series, for instance – throws, with a message naming both the method you called and the kind the Queue actually holds. The non-const overloads give a mutable reference, so calling a payload’s own in-place (_-suffixed) methods through the accessor mutates the value the Queue holds.

These are the “I already know the kind, or I’m willing to find out by exception” accessors. is<T>()/as<T>() are the template-based equivalent, and visit avoids the kind check entirely by handling every kind in one call.

This is also how most Queue work actually gets done: Queue itself only has a handful of methods, but series()/note()/timeline()/duration() hand back the real, full Series/Note/Timeline/Duration object, with its entire own method surface – not a restricted or Queue-specific view of it. Chaining straight off the accessor, as in q.series().mean() or q.note().upper(), is the ordinary way to call any method those four types have; invoke is the alternative for when the method name itself is only known at runtime.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

A reference to the held payload, typed as Series, Note, Timeline, or Duration according to which accessor was called.

Errors¶

Throws (an exception derived from std::exception) when the Queue’s actual kind() does not match the accessor called. The message names the accessor and the actual kind, for example "Queue.as_note(): payload kind is Series".

Examples¶

Example 1. Calling the matching accessor succeeds; calling a mismatched one throws with a message naming the actual kind.

pluss::Queue q(pluss::make_series({4.0, 5.0}));
std::cout << "q.series().numel(): " << q.series().numel() << '\n';
try {
  (void)q.note();
  std::cout << "q.note(): did not throw\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << "q.note() threw: " << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << '\n';
}

Output¶

q.series().numel(): 2
q.note() threw: Queue.as_note(): payload kind is Series

Example 2. The non-const overload gives a mutable reference, so the payload’s own in-place methods mutate the value the Queue holds.

pluss::Queue mutable_q(pluss::make_series({10.0}));
mutable_q.series().add_(pluss::make_series({1.0}));
std::cout << "mutated through non-const series(): " << mutable_q.series().item<double>() << '\n';

Output¶

mutated through non-const series(): 11

add_ is Series’s own in-place addition. Calling it through mutable_q.series() changes the value stored inside mutable_q itself, not a detached copy. This is the only way to mutate a Queue’s held value – invoke cannot reach an in-place method by name; see its Example 5.

Example 3. A couple of ordinary, non-mutating method calls chained directly off each accessor, one pair per kind. This is a small sample, not the whole surface – see each type’s own reference for the rest.

pluss::Queue series_q(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0}));
std::cout << "series().mean(): " << series_q.series().mean().item<double>() << '\n';
std::cout << "series().sum(): " << series_q.series().sum().item<double>() << '\n';

pluss::Queue note_q(pluss::make_note({"  Ab  "}));
std::cout << "note().strip(): " << note_q.note().strip() << '\n';
std::cout << "note().upper(): " << note_q.note().upper() << '\n';

pluss::Queue timeline_q(pluss::timeline::make("1999-04-17T21:15:23Z"));
std::cout << "timeline().year(): " << pluss::series::print(timeline_q.timeline().year()) << '\n';
std::cout << "timeline().add_days(1): " << pluss::timeline::print(timeline_q.timeline().add_days(1)) << '\n';

pluss::Queue duration_q(pluss::duration::hours(-5));
std::cout << "duration().abs(): " << pluss::duration::print(duration_q.duration().abs()) << '\n';
std::cout << "duration().total().hours(): " << pluss::series::print(duration_q.duration().total().hours()) << '\n';

Output¶

series().mean(): 2.5
series().sum(): 10
note().strip(): Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["Ab"]
note().upper(): Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["  AB  "]
timeline().year(): Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=int32, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1999
timeline().add_days(1): Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
1999-04-18 21:15:23
duration().abs(): Duration(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1)
0 days 05:00:00.000000000
duration().total().hours(): Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-5.0000

strip() and upper() are both non-mutating – each returns a new Note rather than changing the one note_q holds, which is why note().upper() still shows the original, unstripped "  Ab  " rather than building on strip()’s result. The same is true of abs(): duration_q itself is untouched, so the later duration().total().hours() call still reports -5, the original value, not the absolute one. Chaining off an accessor calls that method the same way it would be called directly on the type – it does not change what the accessor returns next time, unless the method is one of the in-place, _-suffixed ones, as in Example 2.
